title: Aph. XIII-XV: Apocrypha defined; historical and didactic Apocrypha
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss: The didactic stand as the book belonging toward Wisdom plus Ecclesiasticus. XV. See there chapter 14 on the Apocryphal books from the beginning through Aphorism 14. the Prayer belonging toward Manasseh, the book belonging toward Judith, Baruch, the Letter belonging toward Jeremiah, the additions in Daniel, Ezra's third plus fourth books, the additions to Esther, the book belonging toward Simon the high priest commonly called Third Maccabees, plus First plus Second Maccabees — the historical stand as the book belonging toward Tobit. These stand as partly historical, partly didactic. XIV. we judge it safest that same the Apocrypha be described from opposition to the canonicals — seeing they stand as not equal to them in thread — and since the history plus reason belonging toward this first name's imposition almost escapes us. On the Orthodox Faith book 4 chapter 18 — they stand as opposed to the testamentary books — Damascene. Apocrypha stand as here so called from a hidden disclosure; finally inserted among the canonical books toward the usefulness belonging toward reading. to that same which the Apocrypha stand as commonly added — not on equal thread — books written indeed by pious plus skilled authors, belonging toward that same which it stands as not yet catholically established whether they were inspired by the Holy Spirit plus directed to this, that same by them they should enlarge the canon belonging toward faith plus life; — these stand as the canonical books belonging toward the Old Testament. XIII.
pass_b_english: XIII. These are the canonical books of the Old Testament, to which the Apocrypha are commonly added — not on equal thread — books written indeed by pious and skilled authors, of which it is not yet catholically established whether they were inspired by the Holy Spirit and directed to this, that by them they should enlarge the canon of faith and life; finally inserted among the canonical books for the usefulness of reading. Apocrypha are here so called from a hidden disclosure; they are opposed to the testamentary books — Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith book 4 chapter 18. And since the history and reason of this first name's imposition almost escapes us, we judge it safest that the Apocrypha be described from opposition to the canonicals — seeing they are not equal to them in thread.

XIV. These are partly historical, partly didactic. The historical are the book of Tobit, the Prayer of Manasseh, the book of Judith, Baruch, the Letter of Jeremiah, the additions in Daniel, Ezra's third and fourth books, the additions to Esther, the book of Simon the high priest commonly called Third Maccabees, and First and Second Maccabees. See there chapter 14 on the Apocryphal books from the beginning through Aphorism 14.
XV. The didactic are the book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus.
source_text: XIII. Hi sunt libri Canonici V.T. quibus non pari filo Apocryphi vulgo adduntur, libri ab autoribus piis quidem & peritis conscripti, de quibus tamen nondum catholice constat, an a spiritu S. afflati & ad hoc directi sint, ut his canonem fidei & vitae adaugeant, libris canonicis tandem interserti ob lectionis utilitatem. Apocryphi hic dicuntur, dia apokalypsin kryphiaian, testamentariis opponuntur, Damasc. lib. 4. de orthod. fide cap. 18. Cum autem historia & ratio primae hujus onomasias impositionis nos fere fugiat, tutissimum judicamus, apocryphos ex oppositione canonicorum describi, quippe quibus non sunt filo pares. XIV. Hi sunt partim historici, partim didascalici. Historici sunt liber Tobiae, oratio Manassis, liber Judithae, Baruchi, epistola Jeremiae, adjectiones in Daniele, Esdrae liber tertius & quartus, adjectiones ad librum Estherae, liber Simonis summi sacerdotis, qui vulgo Maccabaeorum tertius, & Maccabaeorum primus & secundus. Vide ibidem caput 14. de libris apocryphis a principio usque ad Aphorismum 14. XV. Didascalici sunt liber Sapientiae & Ecclesiasticus.
